analysis.one_liner: Raises fines on unsafe toy makers up to $10 million and requires public testing certifications.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: with zero cosponsors, it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much more expensive for companies to violate product safety laws covering toys and other consumer goods. It raised the maximum civil fine from $1.25 million to $10 million, expanded the requirement that manufacturers certify their products meet safety rules, required the Consumer Product Safety Commission to keep a public list of certified products on its website, and let the Commission require testing programs. It was introduced in December 2007, shortly after a wave of recalls of toys with lead paint and other hazards, and referred to committee the same day. It never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Families buying toys and other consumer products, who get stronger deterrence against unsafe products: a company facing a possible $10 million fine has more reason to test for hazards like lead before shipping. It also gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission more flexibility to require testing, and gives shoppers a public list of which products carry safety certifications.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families buying toys and children's products

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum civil penalty for violations under the Consumer Product Safety Act, the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, and the Flammable Fabrics Act from $1,250,000 to $10,000,000, making violations much more costly for manufacturers and importers.

Expands the requirement that manufacturers certify their products comply with safety rules to cover rules under every Act enforced by the Consumer Product Safety Commission, not just the Consumer Product Safety Act, and lets the Commission prescribe reasonable testing programs more broadly.

Requires the Commission to post and maintain on its website a current list of all products for which compliance certificates have been filed, and allows it to publish that list, making safety certifications visible to the public.

analysis.who_pays: Toy and consumer product manufacturers and importers, who would face fines up to eight times larger, plus the cost of testing products and filing certification paperwork with the Commission. Some of that cost could be passed on in prices, and small manufacturers would bear the paperwork burden proportionally harder.
analysis.who_pays_short: Toy makers and consumer product importers

drawbacks.text: The testing, certification, and paperwork requirements would fall on manufacturers of all sizes, and the record does not include an analysis of how heavily small toymakers would be hit relative to large importers.
The bill only changes penalty ceilings and paperwork; it does not add inspectors or fund enforcement, so its real effect depends on the Commission actually using its new authority.
Higher maximum fines deter companies only if they are actually imposed; the bill leaves enforcement priorities entirely to the Commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: much larger fines and mandatory, publicly visible certifications in exchange for higher compliance costs that land mainly on manufacturers. The public-safety benefit is real but indirect — it works through deterrence rather than new inspections or mandatory bans — and the bill offers no help to small manufacturers absorbing the new paperwork. Still, at a moment when toy recalls were a national story, raising the penalty ceiling from $1.25 million to $10 million is a meaningful deterrent, and the costs are the ordinary price of product safety enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Graves introduced the Safe Toys Act on December 4, 2007, as the sole sponsor, with no cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to its Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken: the bill stayed in subcommittee for the rest of the 110th Congress and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a vote by the full House.

The bill would have raised maximum civil penalties under three product safety laws from $1,250,000 to $10,000,000 and expanded certification and testing requirements enforced by the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy and consumer product manufacturers, who never faced the $10 million penalty ceiling or the expanded testing and certification requirements. Shoppers got no new protection from this bill, though Congress addressed toy safety through other legislation in 2008.

for.name: Rep. Sam Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 4, 2007, proposing to raise product safety fines to $10 million and require public listing of safety certifications.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Subcommittee of House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the record shows no pattern of support or opposition by party; the sponsor was a Republican introducing a consumer-safety bill.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their maximum fine from $1.25 million to $10 million and required testing and certifications transmitted to the Commission. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran directly against the public's interest in safer toys.

Importers of toys and other consumer products would face the same expanded certification and testing rules and larger fines under the laws the CPSC enforces. Retailers benefit indirectly from a public list of certified products when vetting suppliers.
